name: Sea buckthorn oil

lead: Sea buckthorn oil is taken from the berry pulp and seeds of Hippophae rhamnoides, a hardy shrub of Europe and Asia. The pulp oil is orange to deep red, rich in carotenoids and palmitoleic acid, while the seed oil is richer in linoleic and alpha-linolenic acid.

It is added to creams, lotions and supplements and is promoted for skin repair and anti-aging. Published human studies cover dry eye and other mucosal conditions; a skin-aging trial was registered, but no published human skin results were found.

paras: Proponents attribute its effects to carotenoids, vitamin E, sterols and unsaturated fatty acids with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity. Laboratory work on human skin cells found that seed oil altered lipid metabolism changes induced by UV exposure.

Reviews describe the oil as generally well tolerated in the trials cited, but safety data specific to cosmetic use are limited. It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient and food supplement; regulatory status varies by country.

lead: Sea buckthorn oil is a golden-orange to red oil obtained from the berries, seeds and sometimes leaves of the shrub Hippophae rhamnoides (now also classed as Elaeagnus rhamnoides), native to temperate Europe and Asia.[1][2] Pulp oil and seed oil differ in composition: pulp oil is rich in palmitoleic acid and carotenoids, whereas seed oil is richer in linoleic and alpha-linolenic acids.[3][4]

The oil is used in creams, lotions, hair products and dietary supplements, and is marketed for skin repair, hydration and anti-aging.[2] Human trials of the oil have mostly examined oral use for dry eye and mucosal dryness; one trial of oral and topical use on skin aging was registered in 2008.[5][6] Reviews describe much of the other evidence as preclinical.
infobox: Carotenoids, vitamin E, palmitoleic acid, sterols
Tibetan, Chinese, Mongolian and Russian medicine[2]

paras: Reviews describe the oil as containing a wide range of active compounds including carotenoids, tocopherols, sterols, and polyunsaturated and monounsaturated fatty acids.[3][4] Reference sources report pulp oil at roughly 1.5 to 3 percent of the fruit and seed oil near 11 percent of seed weight, with beta-carotene the main carotenoid.[7] The fatty acid profile of developing berries and the mature seed has been characterised in detail,[8] and the oil has been compared with other unconventional plant oils for cosmetic use.[9] Its xanthophylls have been studied for bioaccessibility.[10]

Sea buckthorn oil is incorporated into hand creams, shampoos, massage oils and moisturisers.[7] Marketing and reference accounts credit it with moisturising, soothing and anti-aging effects; the Grokipedia entry additionally describes wound- and burn-healing claims, which that source attributes to reviews.[2] Laboratory work found that seed oil modified UV-induced changes in lipid metabolism in cultured human skin cells.[11]

Accounts describe use of the fruit and oil in Tibetan, Chinese, Mongolian and Russian traditional medicine for wounds, burns and digestive complaints.[2] The oil is also used as a food colourant and supplement.[2] Reviews have discussed possible health effects of its fatty acids and compounds, including cardiovascular and anticancer research, much of it preclinical.[4][12][13]

A double-blind randomised trial of 86 completers found that 2 g daily of oral sea buckthorn oil for three months was examined against placebo in people with dry eye, assessing tear osmolarity and symptoms.[14] Registered trials on ClinicalTrials.gov include oral and topical treatment for skin aging (n=60, status unknown),[5] effects on mucous membranes (n=116),[15] dry eye (n=100),[6] and eye health with lutein.[16] A flavonol-focused human study examined absorption and cardiovascular risk markers using sea buckthorn products.[13] No published results of the skin-aging trial were found among the sources, and no controlled published trial on facial appearance was found.

timeline.event: Tibetan medical text Somaratsa is reported to describe use of the fruit and oil.[2]
Soviet researchers are reported to study the oil in skincare and nutrition programmes.[2]
Trials on oral and topical oil for skin aging and for dry eye are registered.[5][6]
A randomised trial reports effects of oral oil on tear film osmolarity in dry eye.[14]
